prompt.context: Massive Dynamic is a multi-national pharmaceutical company. One of their assets, Cortexiphan, is an anti-infective that successfully treats three major types of hospital-born illness and is currently in Phase II clinical trials. Unfortunately, Massive Dynamic only has the capital to finance a Phase III clinical trial for one of the three illnesses that Cortexiphan treats. Walter Bishop, Chief Medical Officer of Massive Dynamic, has enlisted your help to decide which of the three possible indications for Cortexiphan they should pursue to maximize profits over a five-year period post-launch.
prompt.question: Which of the three possible indications for Cortexiphan should Massive Dynamic pursue to maximize profits over the five-year period post-launch?

clarifying_info.q: Is there potential approval outside the US?
clarifying_info.a: The drug is only likely to be approved in the US at this time.

clarifying_info.q: How is the drug distributed and sold?
clarifying_info.a: The drug will be sold directly to hospitals by Massive Dynamic; no need to consider distribution channel costs.

clarifying_info.q: Should we use NPV or discounting?
clarifying_info.a: No need to calculate based on NPV; just do total over five years without discounting.

exhibits.title: Market Overview by Indication
exhibits.shows: A table showing number of competitors, market share distribution among competitors, annual doses, and average price per dose for each of the three indications (Candidiasis, Rare Molds, Aspergillosis).

exhibits.title: Cortexiphan Clinical Profile by Indication
exhibits.shows: A table showing Phase III trial success probability, Phase III trial cost, production cost per dose, safety profile vs. market leader, and efficacy profile vs. market leader for each indication.

exhibits.title: Cortexiphan Aspergillosis Formulary Status Distribution by Pricing Strategy
exhibits.shows: A table showing the percentage of hospitals at each formulary status (No Restrictions, On Formulary Restricted, Off Formulary) under three pricing strategies (Discount $5, Parity $10, Premium $15), along with the expected market share at each formulary status.

framework: Identify total market size for each indication (annual doses x price per dose)
Assess competitive landscape and clinical differentiation to estimate realistic market share for Cortexiphan in each indication
Calculate annual profit per indication: (Revenue per dose - Cost per dose) x (Market share x Total annual doses)
Incorporate trial risk: expected profit = (Prob success x 5-year profit) - (Prob fail x trial cost)
Select indication with highest expected profit over five-year horizon
Analyze pricing strategy for chosen indication using formulary status data to optimize revenue

questions.prompt: What are your initial thoughts on the three indications based on Exhibit 1? Calculate total market size for each.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total market size and qualitatively assess competitive dynamics. Aspergillosis: 4 competitors, no dominant leader, decent market. Rare Molds: only 2 competitors, one clear leader at high price ($20), physicians may want alternatives. Candidiasis: very crowded with 6 competitors and no clear leader — will require strong clinical profile to penetrate. Candidate should then request clinical profile data (Exhibit 2).

math.setup: Total Market Size = Annual Doses x Avg Price per Dose
math.answer: Candidiasis is the largest market at $25B, followed by Aspergillosis at $15B and Rare Molds at $4B.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 combined with Exhibit 1, estimate Cortexiphan's likely market share in each indication and calculate annual profits.
questions.guidance: Candidate should link clinical profile to market share. Aspergillosis: superior efficacy vs. market leader, likely to become new market leader (~50-60% share). Rare Molds: equal profile vs. current leader, likely to split with leader but at slight disadvantage as new entrant (~40-50%). Candidiasis: poor safety profile in a crowded market at same price, unlikely to be a significant player (much less than 25%). After discussion, use: Asp=60%, Rare Molds=40%, Cand=10%. Then calculate annual profit = (Revenue per Dose - Cost per Dose) x (Market Share x Annual Doses).

math.setup: Annual Profit = (Avg Price per Dose - Production Cost per Dose) x (Market Share x Annual Doses)
math.answer: Aspergillosis generates the highest annual profit at $2.7B, followed by Candidiasis at $1.5B, and Rare Molds at $1.2B.

questions.prompt: Incorporate trial success probability and trial costs to calculate expected five-year profit for each indication. Which indication should be chosen?
questions.guidance: Candidate must account for trial risk. Five-year profit if successful = Annual Profit x 5 years. Loss if trial fails = trial cost. Expected Profit = (Prob Success x 5-year profit if success) - (Prob Fail x trial cost). Aspergillosis has highest expected profit.

math.setup: Expected 5-Year Profit = (Prob Success x Annual Profit x 5) - (Prob Fail x Trial Cost)
steps: Aspergillosis: 5-yr profit if success = $2.7B x 5 = $13.5B; net of trial cost = $13.5B - $2B = $11.5B; Expected = $11.5B x 50% - $2B x 50% = $5.75B - $1.0B = $4.75B
Rare Molds: 5-yr profit if success = $1.2B x 5 = $6.0B; net of trial cost = $6.0B - $0.5B = $5.5B; Expected = $5.5B x 25% - $0.5B x 75% = $1.375B - $0.375B = $1.0B
Candidiasis: 5-yr profit if success = $1.5B x 5 = $7.5B; net of trial cost = $7.5B - $1.0B = $6.5B; Expected = $6.5B x 60% - $1.0B x 40% = $3.9B - $0.4B = $3.5B
math.answer: Aspergillosis has the highest expected 5-year profit at $4.75B. Candidiasis is second at $3.5B, and Rare Molds is a distant third at $1.0B. Aspergillosis should be chosen.

questions.prompt: Dr. Bishop agrees with the aspergillosis recommendation. He now wants to know the pros and cons of pricing at a discount vs. a premium relative to the market ($10/dose). What are the main considerations?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming exercise. Candidate should discuss both directions.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the effective market share and annual revenue under each pricing strategy for the aspergillosis indication. Which pricing strategy maximizes profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate weighted average market share using sum-product of hospital distribution x formulary-level market share. Then compute annual revenue and 5-year profit net of trial cost. Premium pricing yields the highest profit.

math.setup: Effective Market Share = sum(% hospitals at formulary status x expected market share at that status). Annual Revenue = Total Doses x Effective Market Share x Price. 5-Year Profit = Annual Revenue x 5 - Trial Cost.
steps: 5-year revenues: Discount = $5B x 5 = $25B; Parity = $9B x 5 = $45B; Premium = $11.25B x 5 = $56.25B
Profit tracks revenue since cost per dose is fixed; for Premium: ($15-$7) x (50% x 1.5B) x 5 - $2B = $8 x 0.75B x 5 - $2B = $30B - $2B = $28B
math.answer: Premium pricing at $15/dose generates the highest 5-year profit of $28B (revenue $56.25B minus $2B trial cost). Premium pricing is preferred despite lower formulary penetration.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the main pros and cons of pricing Cortexiphan for aspergillosis at a discount vs. a premium to the current market price of $10/dose?

categories.name: Premium pricing — Pros
ideas: Signals superior clinical value, consistent with Superior efficacy profile vs. competitors
Higher revenue per dose, directly improving margins
Can selectively offer discounts to specific hospitals without sacrificing revenue broadly
Leaves room to lower price later if market share underperforms

categories.name: Premium pricing — Cons
ideas: Worse formulary status and lower market share than discount/parity
Negative publicity given current media and government pressure on high pharmaceutical prices
Hospitals may resist or deprioritize adoption due to budget constraints

categories.name: Discount pricing — Pros
ideas: High market share and faster product uptake
Can capture formulary positions quickly, creating switching costs
Can take price increases over time once established in market

categories.name: Discount pricing — Cons
ideas: Lower revenue per dose reduces margins significantly
Low initial price sets expectations; may hinder future price increases
Pricing choice for aspergillosis could undermine pricing power for rare molds or candidiasis if those indications are pursued later

categories.name: Parity pricing — Consideration
ideas: Middle ground: reasonable market share without sacrificing significant revenue
Still faces competition at same price if not differentiated on formulary access

recommendation: Pursue the Aspergillosis indication for Cortexiphan's Phase III clinical trial; it has the highest expected 5-year profit of $4.75B due to superior clinical efficacy, strong market share potential (~60%), and a large addressable market ($15B total).
Price Cortexiphan at a premium of $15/dose; despite lower formulary penetration, revenue per dose more than compensates, yielding $28B in 5-year profits ($56.25B revenue minus $2B trial cost).
risks: 50% probability of Phase III trial failure, resulting in a $2B loss from trial costs with no revenue
Premium pricing could face political/regulatory pushback in the current pharmaceutical pricing environment
Competitors in aspergillosis may respond with price cuts or increased promotion, eroding market share
A poor safety signal in Phase III (not yet fully known) could further impair market uptake
next_steps: Proceed with Phase III clinical trial design for aspergillosis indication
Develop hospital-level commercial access strategy for premium pricing, including targeted formulary contracting
Monitor Phase III trial results closely; if trial shows signs of failure, evaluate whether capital can be redirected
Assess feasibility of pursuing additional indications (rare molds, candidiasis) sequentially if aspergillosis succeeds
